item.title: We’re not ready for the e/Acc × Longevity preference cascade
item.description:
Anti-aging sentiment might go rapidly mainstream, in the same way AI Safety just did.

Recently, the AI safety community has been enjoying a massive preference cascade that has rapidly moved AI x-risk concerns into mainstream political discourse

Why did this happen?  

  • The basic idea seems like it should have been obvious for a long time: “IF we create self-improving machines that rapidly become much smarter than humans, THEN that seems like that story might not end well for the humans, so we should be very careful.”
  • If the idea is so sensible, why are people only now endorsing it? Proximately, because of HuggingFace, Jacob Coxon, etc. But in a larger sense, clearly the trigger was that the premise (“IF we create self-improving machines…”) no longer strikes people as absurd.  Instead, it seems worryingly plausible.
  • This not only unlocks huge amounts of energy from many new people people thinking the “IF” half of the statement is likely, but also – weirdly, illogically– seems to furthermore cause lots of people to change their minds on the “THEN” half of the statement, too.
  • Why did the flip happen so quickly?  This is actually the case for lots of movements – see Richard Ngo’s truly insightful post “Power Lies Trembling” for much more on the dynamics of preference cascades.

But this isn’t the only preference cascade waiting in the wings, as we continue to scale AI capabilities.  Consider another throwback rationalist classic:

  • “IF it’s possible to cure diseases and slow/reverse the mechanisms of aging, THEN we should do so with the greatest urgency, because death is extremely bad.”
  • Why aren’t normal people on board with this message?  The rationalist in me still burns with frustration at people’s willful obliviousness: “What is the problem?? How can you fail to recognize this!  Do you not AGREE that DEATH IS BAD?”
  • The problem (in the vast majority of cases) is obviously not that normies literally think death is good.  Rather, they think that the first part of the sentence is absurd – everyone knows it’s intractable to make progress against aging.  Those saying otherwise are overwhelmingly likely to be selling snake oil.[1]
  • Thus, few people believe the first part of the sentence is likely.  And this causes them to – weirdly, illogically – reject the second part too.
  • But, AI progress at biomedical research might suddenly make it look tantalizingly plausible that we could make real progress on aging. (Or maybe just, like, cancer. Which would also strike many people as a huge deal.)
  • The resulting preference cascade might unlock prodigious amounts of energy – perhaps much greater than what we’re seeing now with AI x-risk.

The labs are probably working towards this.

Just like the idea of AI x-risk, the hope of using AI to unlock medical cures and other transhumanist goods is widespread among both employees and corporate leaders at the frontier AI labs, rationalists, etc.

Insofar as they aren’t devoting 100% of their energy towards steering to RSI + trying to do some critical safety work along the way (these two things seems to be most of what they’re doing), Anthropic also seems to be steering somewhat out of their way to push medical capabilities – consider for instance how centrally medical science features in Dario’s essay “Machines of Loving Grace”, their detailed coverage of the biology capabilities of each new model, their development of a project-glasswing-style “Life Sciences Verification Program” for qualified access to bioweapons-research-capable models, how they've allegedly opened a wet lab for biology research, etc.  Deepmind also seems to have also devoted a disproportionate amount of effort towards biology research, via efforts like AlphaFold and many others.

Lots of smart people seem to believe that AI-for-longevity is possible, and they’re working hard to make it happen.  Maybe they’ll pull it off!

Although perhaps a cascade wouldn’t happen or would come too late to matter.

Maybe anti-aging is just fundamentally too weird to enter the overton window?

  • I maybe could’ve believed this before, but not after I just saw everyone spin on a time and start talking about risks from uncontrolled AI agent swarms.

Evidence for the tractability of anti-aging medicine might build very gradually and smoothly.

  • As with mathematics – first we’ll see AI making minor contributions, assisting human mathematicians / medical researchers, proving small lemmas / developing new medicines in areas that always seemed especially amenable to AI analysis.  Then only later will we get more dramatic cures that are clearly mostly the result of AI labor, not human efforts.
  • But of course, this slow and continuous buildup of evidence was also the case with AI risk!  Nonetheless the social landscape moves in more abrupt jumps; see again the post “Power Lies Trembling” for why this happens.

A longevity x e/acc movement might simply take too long to gather steam, thus arriving too late to be relevant.

  • If superintelligence comes extremely soon, there’s limited time for weird new social movements to arise and have impact.  eg, if (per the AI Futures Model) we get Top-Expert-Dominating AI that starts churning out serious medical breakthroughs in summer 2028, escalating to superintelligence by winter 2028, that perhaps only provides about six months where anti-aging-related mass public sentiment might be relevant, before the future is essentially decided one way or another.
  • The situation with medicine is quite a bit worse than mathematical proofs that can be formalized in Lean.  In particular, even if superintelligent AI starts delivering unambiguous “millennium-prize-equivalent” medical breakthroughs, there will probably be a fixed time delay while we prove out those experimental treatments (developed in-silico or via laboratory experiments) into actual human patients, via the usual process of human clinical trials.  So there might be, say, a fixed 1-year delay before the medical establishment and general public will accept any given AI treatment as confirmed to work in real humans.  That fixed delay would be very consequential in AI-2027-style takeoff scenarios, perhaps delaying a preference cascade past the point where it could possibly matter.
  • So, this whole analysis is most relevant for medium-term and long-term futures where AI development either intrinsically ends up taking longer than the labs expect, or where we succeed politically in implementing a regime of paced restraint on AI development.

A longevity preference-cascade would be great!  Except, by default, the energies unlocked might flow directly into e/acc  :(

This cultural earthquake, or avalanche, or dam-breaking, catalyzing massive societal energies for the fight against aging, is something that the longevity community has dreamt about for for years.  Unfortunately, the anti-aging preference cascade might, in practice, channel all its energies into AI-accelerationist sentiment.

  • If we start seeing medical breakthroughs unlocked by AI scaling, then it DOES fundamentally make sense to view this, other things equal, as a reason to continue scaling up AI.
  • But on top of that, the companies presenting the results (frontier AI labs, most likely.  or perhaps some biology-specific AI startups) will have every incentive to use this to boost their own PR and public support for accelerating their work.

Before our current AI safety moment, surely there was nevertheless widespread anxiety about humans being replaced by AI.  (See eg the dramatic unpopularity of anything AI-themed in various polls.)  But since the idea of AI x-risk wasn’t being discussed publicly, it strikes me that those worries were essentially being “sublimated” (in the psychological sense) in favor of somewhat vague and incoherent anger about datacenters, flock cameras, copyright infringement, et cetera.  This sublimation process artificially boosted those movements but (until now) greatly weakened public enthusiasm for AI x-risk mitigation.

Right now, humanity’s terror at the prospect of death is similarly sublimated in a variety of ways, since after all there doesn’t seem to be anything practical we can do about it.  But it’s also such an intense terror that it arguably drives a huge percentage of human motivation.

Meanwhile, today’s e/acc movement is honestly kind of pathetic.  Its main argument within the current overton window is just that AI is going to make a lot of money. (“...though not necessarily for YOU, average american worker – I was more thinking about my silicon-valley investor friends.”)  This is enough to convince Trump (at least for now) that opposing AI safety is essential for making sure the stock market keeps going up.  There are a few true e/acc believers who understand that the biggest potential prize is longevity (alongside many other transhumanist goods, like intelligence enhancement). This has little traction with the public, and it seems kind of kooky to even imagine that ordinary people (people like my mom! my neighbors!) might suddenly transform into anti-aging transhumanists.[2]  But this was exactly the state of AI safety discourse a few months ago, when a few experts cared deeply about x-risk but public discussion was an incoherent swirl of mere datacenter skepticism and it seemed crazy that “notkilleveryoneism” would go mainstream any time soon.

Historically, the strength of “e/acc x longevity” has been limited by the fact that most people smart enough to grasp the allure of this idea (eg AI lab CEOs, rationalists, etc) have also been persuaded by the argument for AI risk, and thus for caution despite the allure of e/acc x longevity.  But a future preference cascade among the mass public (cross-pressured by anxieties over superintelligent AI and bioweapons, versus enthusiasm over medical progress) might not play out the same way. So it seems to me that the combination of e/acc ideas, and a mass public that for the first time truly believes in imminent cancer cures, aging treatments and other medical miracles, could end up going in some pretty crazy directions.

IMO the (small, very inside-baseball) controversy over Nick Bostrom’s paper “Optimal Timing for Superintelligence” reflects AI safetyists’ understanding of this dynamic.  “Don’t speak too loudly about this very selfish, dangerous idea!” people seem to be saying.  “If anyone else hears, it might set off the latent anti-aging preference cascade!”  Personally, I don’t think that analytic-philosophy essays (or, for that matter, LessWrong posts like this one) are going to be the match that starts this particular fire.  But the kindling is building up.

Of course I’m not saying we should oppose medical cures!

I’m in a weird position here, I guess. I’m not saying we shouldn’t try to use AI to develop some medical cures. Medical cures are great! (Other things equal, of course. Where “other things” includes x-risk from both reckless AI scaling and from enabling easier bioweapons development.)  Even Eliezer Yudkowsky thinks we should try to go for the medical cures, if we can do so in a responsible way: in his Time open letter of 2023, he says “The moratorium on new large training runs needs to be indefinite and worldwide... If I had infinite freedom to write laws, I might carve out a single exception for AIs being trained solely to solve problems in biology and biotechnology, not trained on text from the internet, and not to the level where they start talking or planning; but if that was remotely complicating the issue I would immediately jettison that proposal and say to just shut it all down.”  Even as he also says that it would naturally be “incredibly selfish and evil” to roll the dice on misaligned AI as described in Bostrom’s “Optimal Timing” paper.

So then what SHOULD we do?

idk!  Here are some thoughts for AI safety groups and funders:

  • Of course there are many variations on the basic core argument “if we die to misaligned AI in the process of rushing for immortality, then obviously we don’t get the immortality!” which will need to be made.  AI safety groups could prepare ahead of time various ways of making that argument convincingly.  But this probably doesn’t take too much preparation; I dunno.
  • Something that might take a bit more advanced planning would be preparing detailed policy roadmaps (along the lines of Yudkowsky’s aforementioned “I might carve out a single exception…”, and analogous to the many current schemes for AI governance, treaty verification, pacing RSI, etc) for trying to defuse the memetic nexus of AI scaling x medical progress, by outlining ways to narrowly focus AI scaling on pushing continued medical progress while simultaneously slowing down more general AI development.

Beyond that, I think AI safety folks might also want to establish some anti-aging bona fides well ahead of time.  Some ideas for how to do that:

  • Today’s pro-pacing and pro-pause AI safety groups often go to great pains to explain that they’re NOT generally opposed to new technology, business, or construction, (eg they favor lots of innovation in nuclear power, lots more housing, are very pro- economic growth and abundance, etc).
  • Similarly, during a future anti-aging preference cascade, the AI safety community will want to be able to point to strong anti-aging bona fides.
  • This will naturally include a record of rhetorical support for the cause of longevity (eg all those classic rationalist blog post).  But should go beyond this to also include (in the case of large funders like Coefficient Giving, perhaps) a record of concrete support for longevity science, political reforms, etc.  For example (and many of these are indeed already funded to some extent by EA/rationalist groups):
    • Detailed political agendas for FDA reform, “clinical trial abundance”, and related ideas about speeding up medical progress.  Including general metascience agendas for improving the efficacy of scientific research generally.
    • Support for actual biomedical science, both relatively mundane (research on cancer, alzheimers, etc), but perhaps in this situation the crazier the better (human genetic engineering, research into the fundamental mechanisms of aging, stuff like antimalarial gene drives for eradicating diseases)
    • Maybe keep a few truly crazy, radical anti-aging ideas in your back pocket, like Robin Hanson’s recent concept of “maybe we should transform our government so it follows a futarchy prediction market focused entirely on trying to bring closer the date we achieve human immortality”.  Just so nobody can try to politically flank you by being more anti-aging than you – you can always pull out your insane plan to completely refocus all of society around longevity, as ironclad proof that (despite your AI safety views) you’re firmly in the anti-aging wing of the anti-aging party.  (You don’t then have to actually implement the insane plan IRL.)
  • It might also make sense to proactively build stronger ties with today’s longevity community.  Fortunately we’re hardly starting from scratch here, as many anti-aging fans, such as Vitalik Buterin, are already very EA-adjacent or rationalist-adjacent.
  • I expect the main focus of an e/acc preference cascade to be focused on medical cures and longevity.  But to the extent that it might also bring other transhumanist goods somewhat into the mainstream, it might be useful to get ahead of the ball on those as well.  (eg things like embryo selection for intelligence enhancement, human augmentation via neuralink-style devices, etc.  though unlike aging research which is perceived as merely kooky, a lot of this other stuff is actively toxic in today’s cultural climate and would be considered a huge PR hazard by most orgs!)

All the above stuff, taken together, sounds like I’m pitching a maximalist agenda for basically transforming EA/rationality into a longevity-focused movement, which would be absurd.  I’m instead just saying that we should consider doing some of this stuff, a little bit more than we already are.

The overarching idea here is that AI safety should be ready to present an alternative vision of radical longevity progress – one that isn’t reliant on breakneck general AI scaling.  This plan doesn’t necessarily need to explain how it’ll actually OUTPERFORM a plan of breakneck scaling at achieving medical progress (which might be unrealistic).  But during a preference cascade, we’ll need to address the issue in some way.  (Just like how it behooves Republicans to have some kind of notional plan even on issues that are unfavorable for them, like healthcare.  And similarly behooves Democrats to make some sorts of commitments on immigration, even if they’d mostly rather people not talk about the issue since it’s unfavorable for them.)  Lest we end up looking like the e/accs do in the current AI safety moment – losing the argument in the eyes of the public, reduced to weak rebuttals, weird ad hominems, and transparent attempts to change the subject.

The “support for FDA reform and scientific research” stuff earlier is important not just so we have a track record to point to, but also because after a longevity preference cascade, there will be strong public demand for taking action on aging.  People will want a roadmap, they’ll want big initiatives being launched and funded, and so on.  So, EA / rationalist groups should perhaps fund some of these things in small-scale now, with a view to being able to impressively scale them up later when the demand arises.  Cryonics also seems particularly relevant here as a shovel-ready plan that acts as a “Plan B” alternative vision for longevity.  Ideally the idea of a crash program to improve the science and scale up the practice of cryonics might be capable of relieving some of the desperate urgency and time pressure that the public might feel about the problem of aging after a preference cascade, and would answer some of the newfound political will to immediately “do something about aging” in a way that doesn’t involve further scaling AI.

What about the labs themselves; what should they do?

  • Whatever AI labs (whether Anthropic, OpenAI, a biology-specific organization like Arc Institute, etc) find themselves in a position to announce newly-developed cures to the world, will have huge amounts of power to frame the ensuing discourse.
    • Consequently, they should think carefully about how to frame their announcements in a way that doesn’t fuel too much desperate e/acc enthusiasm on part of the mass public.
    • Unfortunately, this goal exists in tension with incentives to hype people up about the amazing humanitarian potential (and financial value) of their new technology to the maximum extent possible.
  • Biomedical capabilities come hand-in-hand with scary bioweapons capabilities, so expressing the balance of risks vs rewards in a nuanced way would probably be helpful.
  • Reiterating the fundamental message that “if we die to misaligned AI in the process of rushing for immortality, then obviously we don’t get the immortality!” will also be important for people to hear coming from the labs themselves.

Final thought: in all the above discussion I’ve made it seem like it’s important to have all these plans ready (to channel the energy unlocked by a longevity preference cascade) for the purpose of performing PR judo and deftly deflecting a movement that might damage the cause of AI safety.  But obviously there’s another good reason to have such plans ready in advance: properly directed, a longevity preference cascade could be really great!  It would be amazing to use all that energy for good, using it to fuel more ambitious medical progress in a way that isn’t existentially dangerous.  So, for that basic object-level reason, it would clearly be great to have some shovel-ready plans scoped out for rapidly scaling up ambitious medical research.

  1. ^

    Longevity fans will complain that progress on aging is actually more tractable than the public thinks. I agree! But look at the history of the field: resveratrol? senescent cells? some mouse trials? None of this stuff has produced a genuine miracle for human life expectancy; and meanwhile there have been lots of weird fads and hype. It is very understandable that a distant general public (who has a harder time sifting fads from more promising science) perceives this all as snake oil, or at best overly-optimistic empty promises in the vein of “commercial fusion power is just 10 years away”.

  2. ^

    I’m not sure what exactly how transhumanist a longevity cascade would end up looking like.  Would it mostly be focused on enthusiasm for curing normal diseases, like cancer or Alzheimer, without touching the still-taboo idea of anti-aging?  Could it possibly get crazier than anti-aging, and into other transhumanist goods, like BCIs or etc? Perhaps most importantly, how much would people connect the dots between medical progress and AI policy? Maybe everyone would get excited about medical breakthroughs but this would just translate happily towards pressure for more research funding, FDA reform, etc, without politically connecting to any AI issues? Or maybe people would go full on "worship the coming machine god" at the first whiff of some new AI-developed antibiotics for treating hospital staph infections, or whatever. Who can say!

item.title: A class of statement between conjecture and theorem
item.description:
Parts of the math community, such as Henry Cohn and Grant Sanderson, are arguing that proofs have been a proxy for understanding, and now that proxy is broken. This is a response to LMs generating incomprehensible proofs, often formalized in Lean. While the proofs are verified, they lack the pedagogical value which has historically come along with new proofs. In the past we could typically assume at least one human in the world understood the novel insight required to produce a proof[1], but that assumption no longer holds.

I suspect we will need a new class of statement which contains statements which are proved but not understood, something the mathematical community can formally recognize as a contribution to the field. The understanding gives us the tools to do math, and the proof verifies that our understanding is correct, so we should ensure we have the language to communicate the state of both.

For now I will call this class of statement a compertum (Latin, neuter of compertus, ascertained; from comperire, to find out for certain). A conjecture is from the Latin conicere, to throw together: an inference assembled from the evidence. A theorem is from the Greek theōrēma, that which is looked at or beheld, from the same root as theory and theater. A compertum is something ascertained but not yet beheld, logically sitting between a conjecture and a theorem, a statement whose truth is known but not yet understood. I am curious what name the community lands on.

A recently resolved Erdős conjecture is a good example of a statement which moved from a conjecture to a compertum to a theorem. In April, Liam Price prompted GPT-5.4 Pro with Erdős Problem 1196 (a conjecture) and posted the resulting proof sketch to the Erdős Problems forum. The sketch was correct, and was then formalized in Lean (now a compertum), but the proof strategy was unfamiliar to people who had worked on the problem. In May, a paper by Alexeev, Lichtman, Tao, and five coauthors converted the sketch into a general method that the authors could explain and reuse (now a theorem), and with it proved a second Erdős conjecture and created a short new proof of the Erdős Primitive Set Conjecture. The transition from compertum to theorem was significant even though the statement was already proved: the understanding produced proofs for other problems.

One difficulty is measuring when a proof is understood, identifying that threshold for when a compertum passes into being a theorem. If we want to keep with the historical measure, as long as a person can write a correct proof on their own, then we know at least one person understands the proof. I think an interesting alternative would be an explainer (paper, blog, video, etc.) from which a peer reviewer can write a formal proof.

How exactly we define the threshold between this new class of statement and a theorem needs more thought, but I expect the existence of a new class of statement will become increasingly useful as proofs become increasingly opaque.

  1. ^

    There have been computer-assisted proofs in the past, such as the Four Color Theorem and Hales's proof of the Kepler conjecture. In those cases a human reduced the problem to a large number of simple cases, which a computer then checked. That is closer to using a computer as a calculator than to a computer generating the insight a proof requires. This is a continuum, of course. Computers are now used for everything from evaluating expressions to finding and applying techniques from distant areas of math.

    We also have proofs which are the result of such large collaborations that no individual understands the whole proof, such as the classification of finite simple groups. This looks similar to mathematics as a whole: no person understands the entire field, but each step between lemmas and theorems is understood.

item.title: Gratitude and the End of the World
item.description:
I often try to understand the forces pushing the world towards AGI development despite the risks. It is clear that there are a bunch of different motives. There are market forces and national security competition, but I wonder to what degree we can attribute AI development to a deep dissatisfaction with the world as it is and a desire to transform it even at the cost of much risk. There is a great deal wrong with the world. But if we focus only on its problems, we may develop a distorted picture of what we are risking. To judge correctly, we also have to notice what is good and worth preserving. If we move forward recklessly, what do we stand to lose? Sunsets, dogs, friends, cookies, and infinitely many other small and precious things. Perhaps, if we cultivate gratitude, we would be less willing to gamble it all away.

item.title: Weight smuggling likely defeats attempts to cap FLOPs per training run
item.description:
Epistemic status: >90% confidence in the principle, >70% confidence that mitigating these would be hard in practice, no full implementation yet.

tldr: it seems difficult for verification mechanisms to prevent chaining runs together or aggregating parallel ones; per-run FLOP caps could thus be covertly bypassed.


1. If governments want to regulate frontier AI training, one might want to cap individual training runs, e.g. putting bounds on the number of FLOPs per training run, and making sure each run starts either from scratch (i.e. random initialization at pre-training) or from a known model with accounted FLOPs (e.g. post-training, continuous pre-training, etc).

In the former we could have the initial weights generated by the verifier in some way, or ask for a proof that the weights were initialized with a verifier-controlled random seed. In the later we could ask for a proof that the weights corresponds to unaltered registered weights[1] from a previous training run.

This approach would allow to enforce agreements or regulation targeting a specific model (or model generation) based on FLOPS thresholds: triggering specific evals beyond a specific threshold and possibly proving that a hard threshold has not been reached.


2. However, it seems that there exist many techniques the trainer might use to covertly (a) chain sequential runs together or (b) aggregate parallel ones.[2]

Chaining works by finding a way to inject, at the beginning of the training, the weights of a previously trained model, either to replace a random initialization (pre-training case) or to replace declared weights with ones from bigger training run (post-training case).[3] One way to approach this could be to encode the smuggled weights in the training data[4], decode them when the run begins, then continuing with "normal" training. Some of those techniques might be computationally very similar to regular training.

Aggregation works by combining the results of several parallel runs a posteriori, such as through model souping.[5]


3. Thus, the effectiveness of regulatory regimes which rely on capping the number of FLOPs per training run is in question.[6]


4. A potential solution to avoid this type of attacks consists in not relying on per-run compute budget, but instead on a unique global training budget covering the entirety of the training runs. While preventing that type of attacks, global training budgets approaches still require the questions of global budget thresholds estimation and allocation to be addressed.


GPAI Policy Lab is building a research community tackling open problems in frontier AI verification. If you're interested in contributing, reach out!

  1. ^

    Registration does not imply revealing the weights. A cryptographic signature (e.g. hash) can be publicly registered with a traceability certificate linking to the training run that produced it.

  2. ^

    Such attacks would technically respect the letter of the FLOPs bounds, not the spirit. One might be able to mitigate these by adding restrictions, checking stronger properties of training (beyond literal FLOPs bounds), and putting strict controls on model weights; we're not sure these mitigations can be effective against very competent adversaries.

  3. ^

    This injection does not require necessarily to inject the exact weights: getting close to previous weights could be enough.

  4. ^

    Smuggling the full parameters suite at full precision is likely to require a very big part of the training data, questioning the efficacy of this solution, but a LoRa approximation would make it much more easy to conceal, and unfortunately very tractable.

  5. ^

    Maiti, Shalini, et al. “Souper-Model: How Simple Arithmetic Unlocks State-of-the-Art LLM Performance.” arXiv:2511.13254, arXiv, 17 Nov. 2025. arXiv.org, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2511.13254.

  6. ^

    Let us emphasize that these attacks do not depend on the technical way one verifies FLOPs bounds, unless the technical mechanisms are explicitly designed to try and mitigate the issue, as gestured at in the note above.

item.title: Grantmakers: Consider sharing rough probabilities & brief feedback with grantees/applicants
item.description:
Some thoughts based on some personal experience,[1] something I think could make people and  organizations who depend on grant funding are more effective. Maybe particularly salient now, given the fast pace of AI development. Much of this also applies to employers as well as to ongoing funding relationships, not just grants.  

Costs of applying, incentives to invest in polish

Funding calls and grant applications impose substantial costs on applicants, cutting into the total effective value of the resources that ~"EA can deploy". A lot of work goes into prepping applications, making them look good, and making strategic and stylistic adjustments that aren't always aligned with adding value to the project, the ecosystem, or the world. The worst case is something like an all-pay auction, where in equilibrium the applicants between them invest something close to the full value of the grant in preparing their applications.[2]

Of course, there are also costs on the other side: it can take a lot of time for funders to process and adjudicate these applications.   

I think the EA grantmaking ecosystem does an OK job of holding costs down: short forms, word limits, applications presented as "just give us a first picture of what you do and why." But there's an unavoidable minimum-friction floor when substantial money and personal interest are at stake. Even a mostly effective-altruism-aligned and rationalist applicant has some personal interest, and also may tend to overvalue their own cause and approach relative to a perfect Bayesian (~winner's curse behavior). So it makes sense, from a private PoV, to tweak and optimize extensively.[3] 

Planning and calibrating 

There's a second aspect here. Once you've submitted, or while you're working through a grant and waiting to hear about renewal, you don't know whether you're far above the bar, far below it, or close to it. I made this point in a comment a couple of years ago: applicants may waste a lot of time exploring a very dark space. They don't know when to give up, how much to build fallback plans, how much to adjust the proposal, or in what direction.

A lot of this cost is in planning. If funding is very unlikely, the right move is to get on with the small, low-budget version of the work right now. If funding is likely, that same effort is better spent preparing to move quickly at scale: contractors, staff, compute. With short timelines on AI risk, and salient, actionable, high-impact work to be done right now this matters more. 

The cost of this uncertainty can particularly impact coordination and/or movement building. The people around an organization (volunteers, contractors, allies. etc).  who are deciding how much to engage with it are deciding blind too, and in spaces with several overlapping initiatives, nobody can tell which ones to coalesce around.

It also imposes avoidable costs on the funders and grantmakers themselves. ~The less certainty a nonprofit has about grant funding, the more likely they are to apply for additional grants, sometimes multiple streams from the same granter, which must be processed and adjudicated. Caveat:[4]

This applies beyond the period when an application is pending, which, to be fair, can be reasonably short if planned well. It applies at least as much to organizations you're already funding. Over the course of a grant, I imagine funders form and revise their views: what's going well, what they're having doubts about, how likely they are to renew. Grantees mostly don't see any of that until the renewal decision. If there were some light in this darkness, this would help the grantee prioritize and plan during the grant.  I'd love to asee a place a grantee could check for the funder's current assessment , an updated probability of further funding.

Also high-value: some notes on the things the funder is uncertain about and would like explained or justified better – this  can make aan eventual renewal application more concise and more useful to the funder too.

Funders could  consider sharing 

... both while an application is pending and during a grant:

A rough probability. "We currently predict a 65% chance you get this at your median request or higher." This can be given explicitly as a quick impression, explicitly noisy.   It could even be an AI's take based on context that is not shared with the grantee; tell  an AI or agent something like\

Check our notes and correspondence on the XYZ grant and predict the probability we renew it, and the distribution of funding in expectation. Do a scheduled update every 2 weeks, 
1. Post it on the following password-protected (or anonymized) Grantee Checkin page which we will share with the (potential) grantee.
2.Update us with your rationale for  that in our "Grantee portfolio space" but do not share the latter outside our organization.
In the latter space, provide your best take on what's most in doubt about the application/organization, and prompt us to decide whether to share this in the Grantee Checkin page as well


Again, I think grantees want to know, in particular, 

  • Their probability of success at different funding levels  
    • And it's OK to say "you're well below the bar and this looks like a mismatch with our goals", ideally providing at least some justification and epistemic basis (but not necessary)
  • What's convincing and what's in doubt, to be able to focus their communication work, and their actual practical work. ~"We're convinced about this part of what you do. We'd want to hear more about that part."
  • Grant decision timelines, and whether things are being delayed

The cost-benefit of doing this

This is not free, and I see some reasonable objections. Still, I think offering quick and course private signals has a pretty good benefit-cost here.

Linch highlights the time and opportunity costs --  I think these costs are substantially lower using AI tools. He hints at emotional and political issues getting in the way, and some fear that applicants would overupdate on feedback based on fast takes: I suspect that most EA-aligned grantees/applicants are not too vulnerable to this. And it's ameliorated by carefully generated epistemic status. "This was a probability generated by AI based on our unshared notes" also seems much less likely to lead to overupdating. 

Theere are other issues involving information cascades: these mainly only apply if the feedback is made public or widely shared, not if it's only shared with applicants and grantees.  (Okay, I'd be a bit careful with this:  a specific number like "30% likely to pass our bar" is perhaps more portable and legible, so perhaps more likely to leak to other funders and cause these negative cascades.)

I suspect legal issues are less important here.[5] 

Costs don't seem terribly high to me[6].

On the stated precision: I'd rather funders gave their best guess at a number and made clear it's rough than withheld it. People in this ecosystem are used to estimates like "67%, low confidence" by now, and I doubt many will mistake one for a precise, calibrated forecast. But if buckets (likely, unclear, unlikely) feel more comfortable, that's still much better than nothing. Giving a base success rate also helps. 

Anyone doing this/willing to try it?

Curious: To what extent are funders doin this? Would any funder be willing to try the explicit forecast part? I think even a probability plus an expected decision date, sent at a fixed point after submission, and a light quantitative check-in and steering in the middle of a grant period seems better than silence.  I'd be glad to help design or evaluate a pilot, and perhaps it's something I could help trial and facilitate in context related to my work.

  2. ^

    I let AI remind me/check about the game theoretic and actual game theory results and economics experiment lab evidence :

    The all-pay auction is the right analogy rather than the war of attrition: both are contests where losers don't get their effort back, but in a war of attrition everyone pays the losing bid, since the contest stops when the weaker party concedes, whereas in an all-pay auction each player pays their own bid. Krishna and Morgan (1997) describe them as second-price and first-price all-pay auctions respectively. Grant applications are the first-price case — nobody gets a refund when a rival gives up. 

    On magnitudes: in the standard complete-information models, expected total expenditure can't exceed the prize, since a player who can bid zero must earn non-negative expected profit, and summing that over players bounds total spending by the prize value. Baye, Kovenock and de Vries (1994) prove this for the Tullock contest at every returns-to-scale parameter, and attribute earlier over-dissipation claims to non-equilibrium solutions.

    What does exceed the prize is realized spending: the same authors (1999) show the probability of ex post over-dissipation is one half with two players in a perfectly discriminating contest, falling to about 0.44 as the number of players grows. Experimentally it's worse than the theory — Dechenaux, Kovenock and Sheremeta's survey reports total effort "often twice to five times higher than the common prize value," and Sheremeta puts the median overbidding rate at 72%. 

    Two caveats in the other direction. First, the full-dissipation result belongs to the symmetric mixed equilibrium; the complete-information war of attrition also has asymmetric pure-strategy equilibria that burn nothing (Hendricks, Weiss and Wilson 1988), and Georgiadis, Kim and Kwon (2022) argue the mixed equilibrium doesn't survive adding noise to payoffs. Second, with asymmetric valuations the strongest contestant keeps positive rents and dissipation is incomplete, bounded by the second-highest valuation. Applicants to a given fund are very heterogeneous, so I'd expect real dissipation well below 100% — which is why I say "something like" and don't lean on the equilibrium result. ↩

And refining applications down to the precise right word or character count might be a fun exercise for wordsmiths, but it's a time-consuming one.

item.title: Mech Interp is a Verifiable Task
item.description:
If we think parts of MLP0-MLP3 are computing [a sorting algorithm], we can replace those parts with [a sorting algorithm] and check reconstruction loss.[1] However, reconstruction loss is not enough.

Suppose we replace MLP0 with two things:

  1. Its mean activation - simple, but poor reconstruction
  2. MLP0 - perfect reconstruction, but no reduction in complexity

We can visualize this as a pareto frontier trading off reconstruction with "simplicity". Ideally we achieve perfect reconstruction with perfect simplicity.[2] For more intuition on the pareto frontier, we could have an MLP that clusters all inputs in two clusters: "early positions" and "late positions", which would be slightly more complex than the mean.[3]

We can make this an RLVR environment, if only we could clearly...

Define "Simplicity"

Defining simplicity has been complex. But what do we want from a perfectly decomposed model? If we've "perfectly decomposed" a model, then I'd expect ideal circuits to fall out, with "ideal" meaning:

  1. Help predict OOD behavior
    1. Given an [addition] circuit, we can know which types of inputs it'll succeed & fail on (and why)
  2. Be extractable & minimal
    1. The smallest part of the model that does [addition]
  3. Be removable w/ minimal harm to unrelated circuits
    1. Affects [addition] but not unrelated tasks like [bracket closing]

Currently, I believe we want "circuit simplicity" defined as having a small number of nodes and edges:

  • Nodes - variables like "numbers", "dog-like", "within quotation marks"
  • Edges - causal links. Ideally "dog-like" is computed by a small number of earlier features (eg "dog ear", "dog tail", etc).

Additionally, an ideal decomposition should tell us which features are reused. If two nodes affect all the same downstream nodes, then you can combine them. This reduces both the number of nodes and edges (similar to refactoring code).

In contrast, a complex, dense graph would be two MLPs.

MLP = D(ReLU(Wx))

We can define the "nodes/features" as the hidden dimension:

Nodes = ReLU(Wx)

These nodes are bad because they're polysemantic: they have different meanings at different activation ranges.

When you look at which Nodes in layer 1 are causally important for Nodes in layer 2, it's a dense graph (ie each node is caused by a large number of previous nodes).

Tensor Networks Don't Solve This Issue

In the simpler case of two bilinear layers, you can simply matrix multiply them together and see exactly which hidden dimensions/nodes of the first cause the second directly from the weights. Sparse connections can even be directly optimized for this way.

HOWEVER, we still have a dense graph. The main problem here is our model isn't basis-aligned (ie each coordinate of activations being monosemantic).

With that said, I believe that tensor networks give us better tools to find the correct basis, I am simply too confused atm to make the most of it.[4]

Red Herrings of Simplicity

  1. Bits of information - You can quantize a model into fewer bits of information (float32 to float16), but I won't understand the model better than I used to (so is a bad metric as stated).[5]
    1. Alternatively, I do think an MLP mapping inputs into two clusters is indeed simpler than one that maps to 50k clusters which feels like bits-of-info related.
  2. Low Rank - If my mlp only writes to/reads from a rank 20 subspace, that seems useful to know (because it constrains what other MLPs/attn heads it interacts with) but it's not simpler.
    1. eg If I know a part of the model does [parity], then it's not important if it's rank 2 or 20. If they're caused by the same number of upstream components (and vice versa for downstream components), then that's same number of edges.
  3. Low Features per Datapoint - SAEs & PD (parameter decomposition) care about this. PD cares about the smallest number of "mechanisms" for the full computation path input-to-output.
    1. On its own it fails (define the whole network as 1 feature); you also want a small number of total features to choose from. In hand-wavy terms, we want a simple dictionary (choice of features) and for datapoints to be simply explained, conditioning on that dictionary (...I think?).
  4. Functional Complexity (?) - I have bilinear layers that are a sum of 1k quadratic equations. Maybe you only need 200 quadratic functions and the rest can be approximated as linear (I think this is helpful, but am unsure).

How to Gain Tractability

If we know how models represent [redundancy, circuit suppression, compositionality, hierarchical structure, DAGs, etc], we can decompose modules by just looking at the weights (using tensor transformers). But we don't know those things, so we don't know the right ontology to use when defining "simplicity". There are ways we can gain traction though!

Tract 1: Death Success by 1000 Circuits

With many circuits in a real LLM, we can find components that are shared across circuits. They might read from the same subspace (activation-based) or use the same MLP (weight-based). However, whole MLPs (and whole attn-heads) are the wrong fundamental units to use. Two circuits may use the same MLP but different parts of it.

If we understood which parts of an MLP 1000 circuits shared and didn't share, then that'd be our decomposition. We would then have a ground truth label for how we should've decomposed that MLP eg "Oh there's clearly some hierarchical structure here once you see how it interacts with later attn-heads". Then we can directly decompose the model from the weights from the beggining, with all the circuits falling out naturally.

Tract 2: QK OV Circuits but for Everything

In Anthropic's Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits, they introduced QK & OV circuits. They stopped there because you can't compose other parts of the model together due to nonlinearities such as softmax or GeLU. With a tensor-transformer, you can compose everything with everything, such as embedding --> attn_0 --> mlp_0 --> unembedding.

We can compose any intermediate attn/MLP components together, for any computational path through the network, forming a new sub-tensor that is that computational path. That sub-tensor might have structure (hierarchical, DAG, etc) that individual components didn't.

This property of compositionality is extremely powerful!

Another way to take advantage of this is to take a specific vector from:

  1. An unembedding row (eg "myself")
  2. An unembedding diff (eg "myself" - "yourself")
  3. Classes in the unembedding (eg numbers "1", "2", ... might be in a similar subspace)
  4. Steering vector

You take that vector/subspace and make that the end point of your computational path (ie you can matrix-multiply that vector with any intermediate matrix from Attn_out or MLP_out). Tensor transformers allow you to specify precisely any hypothesis, BUT they don't tell you which hypotheses you should consider, hence I haven't solved mech interp yet.

Tract 3: Interpreting Small Models

We can have small models trained on algorithmic tasks (algzoo) which already exhibit many behaviors we don't know how to approach. For example, training on CE loss on softmax-ed logits incentivizes circuit suppression: bird features can upweight the "bird" class AND/OR downweight other classes. It's more about a class's relative logit value compared to other classes than its objective value. AFAIK, we don't have a solid understanding of how models represent this.

Additionally, models are likely a mix of compositional functions/features and memorization/look-up tables. We can directly tackle this like Linda Linsefors does by training a toy model of memorization. This allows us to better analyze the model in silico as well as build out tools to detect and tease out the structure, while varying hyperparameters.

Again shoehorning tensor networks, if we can state our hypothesis as a tensor, we can directly compare from the model weights whether they're equivalent.

Big if True

If we can deconfuse ourselves enough, we can fully realize mech interp's potential as a verifiable task. This would be a big deal!

We can train models of varying layers, model width, datasets, taking checkpoints and THEN get SOTA models to solve this with RLVR. With enough data of models being reverse-engineered, we can solve training dynamics, how data leads to algorithms, task-ai, etc.

We'll still need to solve value-alignment, of course, but maybe that could be a tensor network too?[6]

If you would like to help in this project, you can always dm me here or on discord at #loganriggs. I'm currently working out of this repo trying to reverse engineer the 500M parameter tensor transformer I trained last year.

item.description:
AI has taken over this blog.

I have moved to a schedule of seven posts per week, and I still cannot keep up.

We still refuse to abandon the rest of the world. Who knows when I will get to post some of my huge backlog on education or dating or other such topics. But the monthly is a sacred tradition. We continue.

Bad News

A good reminder that most news is bad news, and chosen because the bad news in question is rare, which is good news, but the pattern overall of choosing this to be news is bad news, and often the bad news is that the bad news was chosen as news and now people are talking badly about it.

Alibaba uses your computer’s audio system, and other tricks, to at least try and assign you a device fingerprint.

Things you cannot buy in America at any reasonable price. Mostly it is impressive how little makes the list, how it feels like corner cases.

The one thing I am envious of is the exterior roller shutters, and the ability to be in actual pure darkness on demand. I would pay quite a bit to get that, if I could integrate it into my apartment.

Wrong answers are a skill issue.

shellac! in the bay!: what does telling someone “skill issue” mean
A: “you’re doing this wrong, this is pretty easy to fix if you actually try”
B: “there are good returns to being more skilled about this”

Aprii: if you tell someone “skill issue” it’s A but if you describe something as a skill issue it’s B.

I see this as being both A and B at different times.

It turns out that TSPI’s polling was outright fraud, with their explanation fully AI generated. It is a shame that this is not treated as criminal.

Is it a curse?

__eloïse__: The curse of a good trait is that people around you will have it less. Being smart sounds good, but the experience of being smart is being surrounded by retards. Being considerate sounds good, but the experience of being considerate is getting much less consideration from the world than you put out. I think about this when I’m around someone with a lot of rizz. They live in a world of dullards.

That’s true only if you judge relative to yourself. Intelligence, consideration and rizz greatly raise your access to others with intelligence, consideration and rizz, including across such traits. So the question is, are you only thinking in relative terms?

Only about half of all psychology professors said, when asked to pick, that they put social equity concerns before truth, although the rest are overwhelmingly ‘it’s complicated.’ It’s not complicated. There is also a gender divide here, and the OP tries to make it look worse than it is, but neither of those is the story.

I strongly agree with David Perell that it is sad that we used to make it a priority to make a variety of things beautiful, and now we don’t and merely make them functional. The big one is architecture, but this also applies to things like tickets, as per Ted Gioia’s The Banishment of Beauty From Everyday Life.

It’s worse than a crime, it’s a mistake. That beauty buys so much goodwill.

I knew coal plants got people killed but I did not know they also have a lot of radioactivity, or that this is still an active subject of a cover-up.

Nature incinerates what credibility it has left, says ‘the death of Jason Arday must prompt deep reflection.’

Which is the context that means this is not as funny as I was hoping it would be:

This from Jack is a remarkably apt metaphor for the whole situation:

Jack: I work at a famous hospital, one that people around the world visit in order to receive state-of-the-art treatment. My department, cardiology, does vital work every day. We have saved countless lives, and people are right to trust our work. Recently my hospital has been the source of some controversy – some of it fair, much of it overstated.

One of our emergency medicine doctors, Dr. Jones, had fraudulent qualifications, despite work that was broadly respected within his field. A few patients treated by him died preventable deaths in the emergency room. When news media started poking around the story, the hospital ran an internal investigation that cleared him of wrongdoing, and he used legal threats to keep the story quiet.

The story eventually came out when Dr. Williams, who had been previously dismissed from our hospital, documented Dr. Jones’s fraud, kicking up a media firestorm that ruined Dr. Jones’s life. It’s not that some scrutiny was unreasonable – we want doctors to be honest – but the story spiraled far out of proportion.

The attention caused the hospital Dr. Williams works at to reevaluate his position, and it ultimately suspended him and reduced his work duties – reasonably so, because Dr. Williams advocates for unproven and controversial treatments. Leading medical journals have spoken out in defense of Dr. Jones. Other people have raised some concerns about our chiropractic and homeopathy departments, but their work is standard within their fields, and medicine works best when each medical department governs itself.

My hospital is doing fine, actually.

Even among a relatively conscientious group, most people will read private DMs?

Not cool, everyone. I can kind of see arguing the glitch is Musk’s fault, but no.

Focus Only On What Matters

Much failure is about failing to realize what is important. Hindsight sometimes helps, and sometimes it does not.

Ben Vinegar: I recommend people look at indie game postmortems (there’s a lot on Reddit, Youtube)

A recurring theme: “It turns out I was just making games for other indie game devs, and I found out too late they don’t actually buy games”

Rich Uncle Pennybags: i watched a failed cafe post mortem on youtube for whatever reason and the failed proprietor spent more time talking about subtle variations to the coffee due to weather than his decision to locate himself in a commuter town and open at 9:00

the decision to buy the absolute most expensive equipment he could afford and not do anything about the office standard issue grey carpets and unadorned white walls also struck me as questionable.

Woke 1 Was Crazy

Matthew Yglesias points out the arguably worst part of it, which is that even the people who successfully avoided saying absurd or false things were still scared into silence.

Once the reasonable people are running for the hills, everything is f***ed.

Matthew Yglesias: And what I personally remember most bitterly about Woke 1 is not the behavior of the most hysterical people; it’s the behavior of the people who knew perfectly well that others were behaving hysterically and who carefully avoided saying false or insane things (that’s how you can know that they knew) but who also avoided actively contesting them.

This was, for the most part, savvy behavior.

Those who actually said nutty things have suffered for it to an extent, which is exactly why there’s now this effort to slink away from them. But those who ended up on the wrong side of Woke 1 fads also suffered.

The winners were those who ducked the storm — budget experts who knew it wasn’t true that cities spend more money on police than schools but didn’t say so — and emerged with their reputations unscathed.

That incentive structure to avoid being the “well, actually” guy is still very much with us and means that any kind of discourse could go wildly off the rails.

During Woke 1, I very much stuck my neck out with regard to Covid-19, but I was very careful about picking any other battles, and mostly did shut up about everything else. Indeed, I don’t say things I don’t believe, but on a number of fronts I still pick my battles and instead stay quiet.

That was and remains, I believe, savvy behavior, as I would not have gotten much benefit out of the risks and costs I would have endured. If everyone picked one big thing and was loud, that would be enough. But yeah, I still do feel weird about it.

Good Advice

These are two key lessons in spending:

  1. When the price is too outrageous, you want to choke on it, to build good habits.
  2. Focus on absolute price difference, not percentage price difference. Be willing to pay 10 times as much for 10% better, if that’s actually a better deal for you.

Early on you want to focus on lesson one, then later shift to lesson two. Then you strategically and selectively unlearn lesson one.

Armand Domalewski (August 2021): I am 32 years old and still deeply terrified that consuming anything from the hotel room minibar will bankrupt my entire family somehow.

Armand Domalewski (August 2026): Today, I am 37 years old and still deeply terrified that consuming anything from the hotel room minibar will bankrupt my entire family somehow

Jack: Every once in a while when I’m staying at a hotel I think “maybe I’m feeling lazy enough to pay the price premium for a bag of candy or something” and I go up and I ask the price and then back away wearing an expression of combined fascination and horror.

Patrick McKenzie: One of my most indelible I-am-now-officially-old moments was when I realized I was now the target market for the “green car” overpriced shinkansen tickets which, on my first trip to Japan as a student, I was flabbergasted anyone would ever buy.

And as if it were scripted in a movie, next to me at the ticket machine were some twenty-something backpackers commenting on how they weren’t going to be idiots and accidentally hit the Green Car button.

(Green cars are premium cars on the bullet train with slightly nicer seats and a hot towel service, otherwise exactly equivalent to the service in the car adjacent to them, and cost about 50% more.)

The reason the green car can be worthwhile is that the marginal value of the green car is vastly higher than the cost of the train. At some point, one hopes, the train costs you approximately nothing.

What’s the best way to take a break?

How I Write Clips: The 4 elements of an effective break according to Daniel Pink:

  1. Motion beats sitting. A walk restores you more than a chair.
  2. Outside beats inside.
  3. Breaks [for writers] with people beat breaks alone, even for introverts.
  4. Staring at your phone on your walk is not a break. Detach completely. “They’re part of our performance, not a deviation from the performance.”

I buy this, which must be balanced against the cost of the break, and sometimes you really do need an introvert break rather than an extrovert break. They serve different needs.

The question then becomes, detached from what? The phone is not automatically not detached, the same way that being with a person may or may not be detached.

I’ve heard similar versions of this enough that I believe it but I basically don’t get bitten in NYC or Berkeley so it never comes up:

Crémieux: After a month of using it, I can attest:

This thing is magic.

Whenever you get bit by some bug like a mosquito or a sandfly, you just put this on the bite for a few seconds and the itchiness goes away and it heals way faster.

I’m using the Beuer BR90, but it’s the same principle as the old advice to heat up a spoon and put it on bites.

Not at Lighthaven? That is unfortunate for you. You’ll need different norms.

Raye: you can tell how rationalist a subculture is based on how socially ok it is to just walk away from things / conversations / talks

brooke bowman: God it’s so nice I made a point of being weird like that in other spaces too though bc often ppl just don’t even realize it’s an option

Paola: I love that this norm exists. It feels quite liberating, and I practice it relatively regularly when among people who I believe are part of subcultures that allow for it.

HOWEVER, I would never in a million years do anything like this (intentionally) among most subcultures.

There are many social moves similar to this one that I often watch rationalist-adjacent people make among non-rats (eg, saying “I’m bored, “I don’t want to be spoken to right now”, etc.) and cringe each time I see it happen.

For people who want to be taken seriously (or even liked on a basic level) among non-rationalist subcultures, learning how to code switch is one of the most important things you can do. This is especially the case when your standard culture has norms than when applied elsewhere will end up communicating disrespect/disregard for the other party.

General rule of thumb: if less than 80% of the people you’re interacting with are also people you’ve also hung out with at lighthaven, behaving as if you’ve been invited over for dinner with a group Christian Conservatives from the Deep South who are all over 50 will get you better outcomes than behaving as if you are at lighthaven.

I also do not recommend acting like you are with a bunch of Christian Conservatives, which will get you absolutely destroyed among most groups in blue states. There used to be a ‘one generic code’ you could fall back on, and largely be okay. Mostly now there isn’t, because part of the code of one color is reflective dismissal of the codes of a different color. Tricky.

When choosing careers,

Opportunity Knocks

You could instead be at Lighthaven soon.

Inkhaven 3 is coming. If you are thinking about going, you should probably go.

vishal: I’m running Inkhaven 3

Join us Nov 10 – Dec 11 to publish a blog post every day – or begone!

Hone your craft. Get mentored by Scott Alexander, Jesse Singal, Alexander Wales, Scott Sumner, Aella, John Powers, Clara Collier, and more.

First, the facts. You pay for the privilege: $2,000 admission, housing from $1,500. Generous financial aid is available for those who need it (and are daring enough to actually ask for it). Apply at

https://Inkhaven.blog.

You’ll get a decision within 10 days.

Now, I attended both Inkhaven 1 and 2, and am persuaded that Ben Pace and Lightcone have created a magical institution. The image of 40-60 people living together to work on a common craft is a true vision of Utopia. Under these conditions, people become more open, more ambitious, and more creative. You basically get a full year’s worth of socializing crammed into a month. It’s sort of like living in a dorm in the first year of undergrad, but much more intense, and your peers are more mature and interesting.

I was sad when I heard that Ben was considering not running any more Inkhavens, so last week I bumrushed the Lightcone offices and made some demands. And here we are, working together.

The thread has examples of some writing that came out of previous editions, and doesn’t include my favorite of the blogs, which is by Paola, here are some of her posts. I agree with Vishal that the biggest problem so far is that a lot of residents haven’t sustained their writing after Inkhaven.

Alas, I will probably not be an advisor, because when we tried this in Inkhaven 1 it turned out that I was a poor fit, although it would not be impossible to convince me to try again if there was demand.

The University of Michigan robotics curriculum is on GitHub. A second away.

While I Cannot Condone This

I sympathize greatly with Scott Alexander falling into ‘I am staying out of the Substack religion debate [proceeds to get sucked into religion debate].’ This reinforces that if you don’t want to get sucked into a debate, it is often wise to not explain why.

Whenever you hear an 80/20 or other distributional statistic, consider changing ‘Just the top [X]% were [Y]% of [Z]’ to ‘The top [X]% were just [Y]% of [Z]’ and see which one seems more appropriate.

Patrick McGee: Just 20 percent of adults accounted for more than 80 percent of all books read last year. “It’s becoming a kind of niche hobby, like stamp collecting or growing orchids,” Leah Price, a historian of reading at Rutgers University, told [Rose Horowitch].

I would be very surprised if the top 20% of book readers only read 82% of the books. There is an extreme right tail here, and a lot of people read zero.

I too am an Honest Fake Expression Enjoyer:

Paola: I like how noticeably “fake” facial expressions are often actually completely honest, but are just carrying a more specific message. If the goal were deception, it is well within most people’s capacity to fake an actually convincing smile.

However, fake smiles communicate “I’m just being polite and am not actually smiling.” And you’re actually meant to notice all of the information conveyed and behave accordingly.

What I like a lot less are Dishonest Fake Expressions, where the person is acting and trying to present the smile as if it is real, and does not want you to know it is fake.

Know a guy who owns a truck. Then you can move things, or all the things. The cost is buying the pizza afterwards, plus helping out when it is your turn to help. The system works, and it makes everyone richer in a real sense and builds community, but lowers measured GDP. A lot of the story of vibecession and related topics, where economists say you are richer and poor people insist they are instead poorer, is explained by this.

The account here, Nobunaga, has many similarly good stories about a particular American set of norms around community cooperation, reputation, honesty and virtuous norms. I do not take them to be literally true, but this is not important. They are fables in support of norms. Those that have such norms will vastly overperform measured GDP, and people will be happier. Those that lack such norms will underperform measured GDP, and people will be less happy.

The norms are not always efficient, and can be taken too far. The electrician should not be impossible to reach. When you are in higher demand you should charge more, and so on. Growth and productivity rates suffer. I am generally a fan of more capitalism. But something important and valuable is being lost.

If there is going to be an Unexpected Hanging some day this week, what are your options?

Eliezer Yudkowsky: Apply Ultrafinite Recursion:
– The teacher reasons that they cannot give the test on Friday, or students will know.
– The teacher realizes that students may realize the teacher realizes this, ruling out Thursday.
– Humans recurse at most 3 levels, so Mon/Tue/Weds all possible.

Note this assumes a teacher operating at actual max recursion, modeling students modeling teacher modeling students. Less smart teachers, or teachers who model their students as dumb, may give test Thursday.

You may observe that to solve this problem I had to model the teacher modeling the students modeling the teacher modeling the students. I can do this because secretly at WIS 22 the max level goes up to 4.

Robert Garritty: But each iteration of this reasoning starts the recursion back at 0. If Mon/Tuesday/Wednesday are all possible, then Wednesday’s not possible, and so on. This doesn’t resolve the paradox.

Eliezer Yudkowsky: Nope, the teacher could test you on Wednesday and it would be a surprise to you (uncertain) because given that the teacher has already waited until Wednesday, you don’t know whether the teacher is smart enough, or thinks you’re smart enough, that they wouldn’t test on Thursday.

Which in turn, I argue, means you can also test on Friday, because on Friday you will think it would not be a surprise so therefore they can’t give the test, which means it will be a surprise.

item.title: A Brief History of Koinometry
item.description:
As transportation improved and distant villages grew closer, many cultures started standardizing their systems of measurement to make commerce easier. None, however, went as far in their attempts at unification as the kingdom of Enopolis. Their practice, which historians have come to refer to as Koinometry, was based on a single universal measurement unit called the Metron.

This initially posed some challenges, as it was not immediately clear how, for example, one Metron of time should compare to one Metron of distance. To resolve this, a central institution was charged with adjusting the standard unit to each particular context of use.

To keep numbers in a range that was comfortable to calculate with, the unit was eventually adapted not just to the properties it measured, but also to the objects of which those properties were measured. One Metron of money thus referred to a different amount when buying a house than when buying wine at a tavern, and one Metron of length referred to a different distance when measuring out knitting yarn than when describing astronomical measurements.

The incommensurability of the monetary Metron caused considerable confusion, until a council of experienced metrologists arrived at a straightforward simplification: One Metron of money was henceforth to refer to the price of one Metron of the goods being traded.

Thorne (1827) recounts the example of a merchant greatly expanding their business by offering delivery of one Metron of grain annually to households under a standard agreement, while local government metrologists took care of adapting the unit to regionally prevailing household sizes and dietary customs. In the following decade, grain shortages threatened this arrangement, but since consumption fell along with the bad harvest, the Metron was adjusted and contracts could still be fulfilled.

Practices around the measurement of time are of particular interest. At first, the length of a temporal Metron depended only on what kind of time was being measured. A day of idle time might have measured between 20 and 25 Metrons from sunrise to sunset, whereas a feast of similar duration was usually considered to have lasted two to three.

This was eventually deemed insufficiently precise, as people found that uneventful stretches dragged on but compressed in hindsight, and vice versa. It was therefore decided to make the temporal Metron’s length depend not only on the activity it represented, but also on the perspective, multiplying pleasant Metrons of time after the fact and dividing idle ones. The inactive day would thus turn into about five Metrons a week after the fact, whereas the feast might expand to something around thirty Metrons when looked back on.

Employment agreements were eventually exempted from retrospective adjustments based on subjective experience, as the resulting disagreements proved a great burden on the Enopolitan economy. Unger (1837b) reports repeated discussions of defining temporal Metrons of work in terms of their productivity, but this appears not to have been enacted despite multiple attempts at reform.

Karashima (1912) documents a notable legal dispute involving a worker preparing food at the large wedding of a senior administrator of the metrological academy. The administrator’s marriage unraveled over alleged infidelities after five (contemporaneous; this was later adjusted) Metrons. While retroactive adjustments to the worker’s experience of catering to the guests were explicitly ruled out by employment law, he maintained that the failed marriage should change the duration of the festivities themselves, and demanded a corresponding adjustment to his wages.

Several guests had testified that the festivities now seemed less significant than they did at the time, making them somewhat forgettable. At first glance, one might expect this to lower the worker’s pay, since insignificant time compresses in hindsight, and his shift was thus now shorter than if the marriage had worked out. He argued, however, that what mattered for compensation was the contemporaneous duration, which for insignificant time was considered longer than for joyful occasions. The outcome of the case is not entirely clear from the historical record. Although it is known that a settlement was reached for an amount of two Metrons, the value of this cannot be fully reconstructed based on the available information.

The practice of Koinometry flourished for about five centuries (the most accurate duration in Metrons remains contested among scholars). Eventually, the growing inertia of the increasingly complex governing institution appears to have made the Metron slower to adapt to changing contexts of use, while increased economic and cultural exchange in the region accelerated the pace of cultural change. In consequence, its use began falling out of favor as confusion over its correct application grew and increasingly caused friction.

A variety of informal measurement units appear to have emerged during this period. Notably, some of these aspired to Metron-like generality, whereas others deliberately focused on narrow applications in the hope that this would improve their consistency and make them easier to reason about.

Many of the latter units were exceedingly narrow in scope. One example, reported by Nakamura (1887), is that of a unit of volume to be used only for beer brewed from a specific strain of hops and served at a specific temperature. That temperature was in turn given in another highly specific unit only to be used for the same kind of beer, the non-circular definition of which is thought to have existed at the time but has been lost to history. The government at first tried to maintain conversion tables between many of these units and the Metron, but eventually prohibited their use when this became infeasible due to their rapid proliferation.

The ensuing general discontent nearly culminated in what would have been a devastating war over trade-related disputes between Enopolis and two adjacent city-states. However, armies found themselves facing considerable difficulties accurately measuring distances on maps of enemy territory, which not only used different locally defined units, but also often needed conversion between Metrons used for measuring distances on maps and those used for measuring distances on the ground.

Scouts also often reported the length of marches in temporal Metrons, leading to discrepancies between durations reported by someone who had walked alone and someone marching as part of a large unit. This slowed down advances and thwarted attempted attacks, which won some time for diplomatic negotiations eventually leading to a peaceful resolution.

Hansen (1729) reports that considerable effort went into agreeing on exact borders and terms of trade, as conversion factors into a large variety of units used by neighboring countries had to be worked out and documented. The resulting treaty is notable as the only preserved Enopolitan document whose numbers are interpretable without consulting additional metrological tables.
